source.title: From Knots to Knobs: Towards Steerable Collaborative Filtering Using Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Martin Spišák; Ladislav Peška; Petr Skoda; Vojtěch Vančura; Rodrigo Alves

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses sparse autoencoders to obtain interpretable recommendation controls, relying on the idea that SAEs can disentangle polysemantic activations. Its own results concern semantic mappings in recommender models, not the claim versions’ specified polysemantic-neuron questions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures tag–neuron activation selectivity, which is relevant to neuron interpretability but does not directly test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, why polysemanticity arises, or whether polysemanticity depends on the specified factors. Reconstruction and steering performance results are not rows because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The study applies SAEs to collaborative-filtering autoencoder embeddings and measures tag selectivity of SAE latents, not neurons of the base model. It cites the idea that dense activations are polysemantic as motivation but never measures polysemanticity of CFAE neurons, image-classifier neurons or language-model MLP neurons. It does not test superposition causes or architecture dependence. Its selectivity results concern SAE dictionary features in a recommender, a different construct from the versions.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that SAEs inserted into CFAEs yield largely monosemantic, interpretable latents that map to metadata tags, and that TopK SAEs preserve accuracy for cosine-like embeddings. Steering works for ELSA but largely fails for MultVAE when representative neurons are used. Note that these are SAE latents, not the CFAE's own neurons.
record.recipe_differences: The paper inserts and trains SAEs on collaborative-filtering user embeddings, then maps activations to item metadata tags; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron methods or test the original examples.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported selectivity comparisons differ across CFAE/SAE configurations and mapping directions. The paper reports MultVAE+L2 as having the greatest relative entropy decrease, followed by ELSA+Cosine and ELSA+L2; KL-divergence selectivity is described as similar for MultVAE+L2 and ELSA+Cosine, with ELSA+L2 somewhat lower.

fits_no_version.finding: In TopK SAEs trained on collaborative-filtering autoencoder embeddings, many latents show selective tag activation. For example, 88%/59%/88% of tags have D_KL>10 for MultVAE+L2, ELSA+L2 and ELSA+Cosine. Some latents serve several related tags, such as superhero and comic book, or space action and classic sci-fi.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents on recommender embeddings are largely tag-selective (monosemantic by a metadata-based TF-IDF measure). Any multi-tag latents reflect correlated metadata or popularity bias.

record.problems: For the neuron-interpretability results, the study uses one dataset and metadata-based tag mappings; it does not directly test unrelated-input mixtures or independently validate that a neuron has one coherent job. Some reported selectivity results are qualitative, and the paper does not state uncertainty estimates for them.
record.rows_left_out: Reconstruction-accuracy and steering outcomes in Sections 4.2 and 4.4 were left out because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity or the claim versions.

untested.parts: All parts: no language-model MLP neurons.
All parts: superposition is not measured. The study only presumes that SAEs disentangle activations.
All parts: neuron polysemanticity is not compared across architectures. The SAE reconstruction-loss comparisons concern SAE latents, not base neurons.
All parts: canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
All parts: polysemanticity criteria are not varied.

record.verdict_notes: The study's 'neurons' are SAE dictionary latents. It never measures how polysemantic the underlying CFAE dimensions are, so no polysemantic-neuron version is tested. Appendix B.2's multi-tag latents (e.g., id3125, id2491) are attributed to related concepts or popularity bias; this is SAE-level evidence only, not V6.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and mixed visual inputs.
Transformer language-model MLP neurons, unrelated tokens or contexts, and layerwise prevalence.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Whether the share of polysemantic neurons varies with activation function, architecture, or regularization, and whether it can be lowered without large performance loss.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons are misread and instead respond to one shared feature or related jobs.
Whether polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: MultVAE+L2
rows.operation_detail: Measured KL divergence of tag-to-neuron activation distributions.
rows.measure: Share of tag-to-neuron entries with KL divergence greater than 10
rows.note: The authors interpret high divergence as tags having distinctive activation patterns; this is not a direct test of unrelated inputs activating one neuron.
rows.check: Measures KL divergence of tag-to-SAE-latent distributions in a recommender. This is SAE feature selectivity, not base-model neuron polysemanticity. Subject should read 'TopK SAE (k=16, 8,192 latents) on 1024-d MultVAE'.
